analysis.one_liner: Shields manufacturers from most product-liability lawsuits and overrides state laws that hold them accountable.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote in the House; it sat in two committees and a subcommittee until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a uniform national rule letting manufacturers off the hook in most civil lawsuits. A manufacturer could not be held liable for harm its product caused if someone else's criminal or intentional act was a cause of the harm, and it could not be sued over how it sold or marketed a product unless it broke a specific law and that violation caused the harm. It would also override state laws that let injured people sue manufacturers more easily, while preserving state laws that give manufacturers even more protection.
analysis.who_benefits: Product manufacturers across the economy gain, because the bill sharply narrows when an injured person can sue them and eliminates lawsuits over marketing and selling practices unless a statute was violated. Insurers covering manufacturers also benefit from fewer and smaller claims.

how_it_helps.text: A manufacturer would not be liable for harm from its product if a criminal or intentionally tortious act by someone else was a proximate cause of the harm, in any state or federal court.

A manufacturer could not be held liable for harm resulting from the sale or marketing of its product unless it failed to substantially comply with a state or federal statute governing that sale or marketing, and that failure caused the harm.
The bill preempts state laws inconsistent with it, but only in one direction: state laws that give manufacturers greater protection from liability are preserved.

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective or dangerously marketed products bear the cost: they would lose the ability to recover from manufacturers in many situations where state law currently allows it, including cases involving a third party's crime or a sale that complied with the letter of a statute. State governments would also lose part of their authority to set their own liability rules.

drawbacks.text: The marketing-and-sale shield is a compliance defense: a manufacturer could not be sued over how it sold or advertised a product as long as it substantially complied with existing statutes, even if its practices foreseeably caused harm, leaving injured people with no remedy.

The third-party-act shield would block lawsuits whenever another person's criminal or intentional act was a proximate cause of harm, potentially immunizing manufacturers and sellers whose own negligence contributed to that harm.

The preemption is one-sided: it strikes down state laws that hold manufacturers more accountable while locking in state laws that protect them more, removing states' ability to set stricter standards for their own residents.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give manufacturers predictable, uniform liability rules and lower litigation exposure, which supporters argued would ease burdens on interstate commerce. But it would do so by shifting the cost of injuries onto injured people and closing off entire categories of claims, and its preemption runs only in manufacturers' favor, so state consumer protections could not be restored. The scales tip toward manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent it to the Judiciary and Commerce committees, which passed it down to a subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Hostettler and four original cosponsors introduced the bill on April 27, 1999.
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and to the Commerce Committee on the day of introduction.

On May 17, 1999, it was referred to the Judiciary-linked Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection in the Commerce Committee's structure, and no further action appears in the record.
The bill attracted 31 cosponsors but was never reported out of committee, never debated on the House floor, and received no vote before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers and state governments came out ahead: the liability shields and the one-way preemption of state law never took effect, so the existing state-law remedies stayed intact. Manufacturers and their insurers are worse off than they would have been under the bill, though no rule changed either way.

for.name: Rep. John Hostettler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 31 cosponsors for it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral, chaired by Rep. Henry Hyde (R-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out for a floor vote.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of additional referral, chaired by Rep. Tom Bliley (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to a subcommittee, and never advanced it further.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 27 Republicans to 3 Democrats and 1 Independent — and no floor vote ever took place to test broader support.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of consumer and industrial products
industries.note: The bill would sharply cut manufacturers' lawsuit exposure, eliminating liability for marketing and sales practices that complied with statutes and for harms proximately caused by third-party criminal acts. The cost of injuries that no longer compensateable would fall on injured consumers.

Fewer and smaller product-liability claims would reduce insurers' payouts on policies covering manufacturers. Consumers would gain nothing in return except lower litigation costs passed through unevenly, if at all.

industries.industry: State tort systems and trial lawyers
industries.note: The bill preempts state laws that let injured people sue manufacturers, shrinking both states' regulatory authority and the legal remedies available to ordinary people. State laws favoring manufacturers are expressly preserved.
